notes: Attempt 20261026T005124478-ru-mir-01-write-c08. The previous attempt (20261026T001606715) was rejected only for out-of-scope edits: running the checker regenerates content/ru/analysis/glava-01..07 sidecars, because merging this chapter's lexicon delta changes every lesson's input digest. This attempt ran the checker and then restored those seven sidecars byte for byte from a copy taken before the first run, and removed its own analysis/glava-08 sidecars at the end (the runner's check regenerates them).

Written from the frozen plan row: four sections (the cart to the fair; the smith; Ivan and Nastya at the stalls, Fyodor and Silanty at the cart; the argument at the cart, the turn, home and Vera). Timeline: the cart leaves at night («Ночь, и уже́ хо́лодно»), the fair is in the morning (the district town is a day's cart ride, continuity.json); home and Vera's school on the next evening. Problem: three roubles for four needs (four new shoes with the work 2 r., Nastya's slate, Ivan's presents, Fyodor's 3 r. to stay in town and wait for his отруб business). Turn: Pyotr gives his three roubles to Fyodor («Я не за о́труб. Но ты мой сын. Сын помога́ет отцу́, а оте́ц — сы́ну»); the horse keeps limping («Ло́шадь хрома́ет и ждёт», echoing Глава 4's «Земля́ ждёт»); Ivan buys the пряник and then the slate with his own rouble and kopecks. Consequence: Fyodor stays in town with the money («его́ де́ло — не на я́рмарке»; at home «Фёдора нет: он ещё в го́роде») («Мой овёс — твой.» — «Э́то не пода́рок, Фёдор.»); Vera gets no present, Ivan asks her for a book and gets an азбука («Э́то не пода́рок. Э́то кни́га из шко́лы.»).

Present tense throughout (past is G10). Perfectives only as the licensed infinitives купи́ть / прода́ть after на́до / хо́чет, and after не мо́жешь in s091 (no дать / сказа́ть anywhere). Dative singular and pronoun datives only (вам once); no dative plural. No instrumental (у́тром, ве́чером, но́чью pinned as adverbs). Prices only 1–4 with genitive singular (два рубля́, две копе́йки, четы́ре копе́йки); ages through the baseline chunk with лет (12, 19, 70).
Slate continuity: Nastya's mended slate from Глава 2 is the one Ivan uses in Vera's class (Главы 5–6), so Nastya now needs her own («Моя́ доска́ тепе́рь у Ива́на!»); Ivan buys the new slate.

Warnings left, with reasons: recurrence ru-nuzhda (1 use in the story, in the proverb; the row plans нужда́ for the Слово, where it occurs four more times); new-cluster s039 «Мне на́до купи́ть подко́вы… Но и Фёдору нужны́ де́ньги» (на́до and купи́ть are glossed here; нужны́ and подко́ва are already known from s006; splitting would break Pyotr's one turn); stress-unverified (no RUAccent model on this host; stresses set by hand from the lexicon and Главы 1–7 and checked in the language pass); continuity warning on glava-07's log is the runner's merge, not this chapter.

Media: cover and two inline scenes planned (smith holding up one new horseshoe to Pyotr; Ivan counting kopecks at the gingerbread stall); three margin vignettes planned (теле́га, подко́ва, пря́ник), each with a text gloss so that no sentence depends on a planned picture; the dative arrow diagram ru-mir-01-l08-svg-komu.svg is drawn here (Ivan and Nastya as clothed figures in the l02 style, labels 17–20 px in a 300 px viewBox).

Workbook: three exercises per section in sections 1–3, three in section 4 (12 exercises, 72 items); every item one gap with visible help (bracketed lemma or pronoun, first letters, or a choice of two-word phrases); drilled forms appear in the story by the end of their section. Pensum A 10 (2 recall: G06 Кузне́ц смо́трит на Ива́на, G03 нет пода́рка), B 10 with a 13-word bank, C 8 open questions in story order with one Почему́? (c5) and «А ты?» last.

Prices and costs are marked [?] in review_questions: two roubles for a new shoe with the shoeing, one rouble for a sack of oats called cheap, three roubles for the отруб business in town, two roubles for a book at a fair stall. docs/russian-mir-history.md has no 1913 fair prices.

Codex review 1025-181628-32404 (read-only) applied: timeline spread over night/morning/next day; horseshoe price made «четы́ре подко́вы и рабо́та — два рубля́» (Codex cites 60 kop. a hoof in a 1911 Tomsk advertisement) and the confusing old-shoe offer removed; Fyodor's three roubles explained as staying in town to wait; independent infinitive questions reframed («А что ему́ на́до купи́ть…?»; «Ты не мо́жешь прода́ть овёс?»); glosses fixed (что ну́жно? example instead of a false equation; цена́ by example; пьёт во́ду, а ест овёс as examples, not antonyms; се́мьдесят = 70; нужда́: де́нег нет, а хлеб ну́жен; по glossed at its first use по доро́ге); Nastya goes to the smith with the others; им added (Де́ду и На́сте ве́село: им нра́вится пря́ник); x2-1-5 hint, x3-3-3 choices, c6 model, Russian in rubrics stressed; diktant items given first letters as visible help until audio exists.

Codex findings not applied, with reasons: (1) нау́чит in the proverb — the plan row prescribes «Нужда́ всему́ нау́чит»; the segment is a quotation (the course's mechanism, as Глава 7's «Слу́хом земля́ по́лнится»), glossed and never tested. (2) Stress marks in the SVG labels — earlier diagrams (l06 kogo-chto, l07 slukh) carry none and the course strips stress everywhere by default; kept consistent.

review_questions.quote: — Зима́ идёт, — говори́т оте́ц. — Кому́ что ну́жно…
review_questions.question: Pyotr's sigh «Кому́ что ну́жно…» after «Зима́ идёт»: natural as a weary half-proverb, or does it need a fuller line?

review_questions.quote: — Четы́ре подко́вы и рабо́та — два рубля́.
review_questions.question: Price check [?]: two roubles for shoeing all four hooves with new shoes at a district fair in 1913? The plan fixes «two roubles» for a horseshoe; Codex cited a 1911 Tomsk advertisement at 60 kopecks a hoof, so the text makes it four shoes + work.

«Мне нужны́ де́ньги. Три рубля́.» and later «Фёдору нужны́ три рубля́»: is нужны́ with три рубля́ acceptable here, or should a reviewer prefer ну́жно три рубля́? (нужны́ kept to keep the agreement lesson clean.)

review_questions.quote: — На о́труб. Моё де́ло — в го́роде, а в го́роде всё до́рого.
review_questions.question: Fyodor needs three roubles «на о́труб» [?]: the text explains it as staying in the district town to wait for his business («Мне на́до жить в го́роде и ждать: там моё де́ло»); what an applicant actually paid in 1913 is unverified.

review_questions.quote: — Овёс? Рубль за мешо́к, — говори́т Сила́нтий.
review_questions.question: Price check [?]: one rouble for a sack of oats called cheap at an autumn fair in 1913 (a 5-pood sack at 1913 oat prices would fetch more): plausible as Silanty's low offer?
«Ему́ ну́жен пода́рок сестре́» (dative of the recipient after a noun): natural, or prefer «пода́рок для сестры́»? Dative kept for the chapter's target.

review_questions.quote: — Рубль? Э́то не цена́! Э́то дёшево.
review_questions.question: «Это не цена́!» as a peasant's retort to a low offer: idiomatic for 1913?
Present imperfective «покупа́ю» for an immediate decision (perfective future is G13): natural?

review_questions.quote: — Нет, э́то не пода́рок. Э́то кни́га из шко́лы.
review_questions.question: Was «Э́то кни́га шко́лы»; changed to «кни́га из шко́лы» in the audit-fix patch (RU8-05; шко́льная is not yet licensed). Natural?
Proverb given to Silanty, who uses it cynically (need will make Fyodor sell cheap): does the attribution sit right with the Слово, where Пётр, Фёдор and Силантий each read нужда́ differently?

cover.alt: The autumn fair in the district town: carts, horses, stalls, an open smithy and a gingerbread stall, the church dome behind; the Sokolovs arrive on their cart.
cover.art_brief: A Russian district town (уездный город), Ryazan province, the autumn fair, late October 1913 O.S., morning, cold clear light, the first frost on the ground, bare birches. A broad unpaved square crowded with peasant carts (телеги) and horses, sacks of grain on the carts; plain wooden stalls under canvas: one with rows of round brown gingerbreads, one with red kerchiefs hanging on a rail; at the left an open-fronted smithy with a glowing forge and a smith at the anvil. Behind everything a white stone church with a green onion dome. In the right foreground the Sokolovs arrive on their own cart pulled by a bay horse that favours one foreleg: Pyotr (about 50, grey-streaked beard, brown homespun coat, cap) holds the reins; Fyodor (27, dark beard, soldier's bearing, dark coat, cap) sits on two grain sacks; Ivan (19, fair, cap, short padded coat over a red shirt) and Nastya (12, kerchief, padded jacket) sit at the back, Nastya pointing excitedly at the stalls. No text in the image.

exercises.title: Оконча́ния
exercises.hint_en: Type the whole word; the first letters are shown. кому́? — dative: masculines in a consonant, -й or -ь and neuters in -о/-е (сло́во → сло́ву) → -у/-ю; most -а/-я nouns → -е (Фе́дя → Фе́де too); -ь feminines → -и (мать → ма́тери).

inference_aids.art_brief: District-town autumn fair, Ryazan province, late October 1913 O.S., late morning, cold grey light. Foreground: an open-fronted wooden smithy at the edge of the fair, a glowing forge and an anvil behind. The smith (kuznets, about 45, very broad, leather apron over a dark shirt, sleeves rolled, short dark beard) half-crouches with the Sokolovs' bay horse's left foreleg lifted and its hoof resting on his knee; in his raised right hand he holds up one new dark horseshoe towards Pyotr; the worn old shoe is still on the lifted hoof. Pyotr Matveyevich (about 50, grey-streaked beard, brown homespun coat, cap) looks at the horseshoes with a careful, worried face. Ivan (19, red shirt under a short padded coat, cap, fair hair) stands at the horse's head holding the bridle. Behind them, a few steps away, Nastya (12, kerchief, padded jacket) leans bored against a cart wheel. In the background carts and the fair. A wooden pail of water by the horse. No text in the image.

words_with_history.title: Слова́ с исто́рией
text: Нужда́ — де́нег нет, а ну́жно всё: ло́шади — подко́ва, На́сте — доска́, Фёдору — о́труб.
Пётр говори́т: «Нужда́? На́до ждать». Ло́шадь хрома́ет и ждёт, и он ждёт.
Фёдор говори́т: «Нужда́? Так жить нельзя́. Мне ну́жен о́труб».
А Сила́нтий ду́мает: «У мужика́ нужда́ — мужи́к продаёт дёшево».
words_with_history.note_en: Нужда́ is need, want and poverty at once, the root of ну́жно. In 1913 a peasant household paid cash for little: salt, iron, kerchiefs, a horseshoe, taxes. Grain was sold at the autumn fair, when prices were lowest and the buyers knew it. The proverb: "Need will teach you everything."

grammar.title: Кому́? Кому́ что ну́жно?
grammar.rule: кому́? — Петру́, кузнецу́, На́сте, Ве́ре, ло́шади, ма́тери · мне, тебе́, ему́, ей, вам, им · на́шему де́ду, твое́й ло́шади · На́сте нужна́ доска́, Фёдору нужны́ де́ньги
grammar.note_en: The dative answers кому́? "to or for whom?": the person who receives (даёт На́сте), is helped (помога́ет отцу́), is shown or told something, or who feels, needs, may or must (мне хо́лодно, на́до, нельзя́). Endings: -у/-ю for consonant/-й/-ь masculines and -о/-е neuters (Петру́, сло́ву); -е for most -а/-я nouns, Фе́дя too (Фе́де); -и for -ь feminines (ло́шади, ма́тери). Ну́жен/нужна́/ну́жно/нужны́ agrees with the thing needed. Age: Ему́ девятна́дцать лет. К + dative is "towards", по + dative "along, around".
